transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Thank you. Well, I came in today because I’m just tired all the time. It's... it's really starting to get to me. By midmorning at work—I'm a claims adjuster—after just reviewing some files or walking a junior adjuster through a claim, it feels like my body and my brain are already running on empty. I just don't have the energy I should.
How long have you been experiencing this persistent fatigue?

It's been... well, about three years and three months now. It started right around the time I was moved into a higher-responsibility role at work, which is when I had to start mentoring the other adjusters and overseeing our new workflow systems.
Over these past three years, have you noticed changes in your mood—such as feeling sad, empty, or down most days? Or have you lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Yes, I have. Most days, it just feels like... well, like there’s a gray film over everything. Even when things are fine—like if my husband is being really kind, or we’re cooking with the family—I just don't feel it. I go through the motions, but I don't really feel the enjoyment I used to have.
During these three years, have you been experiencing excessive worry or anxiety about things—like work situations, your health, or other concerns—that feels hard to control?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, work is stressful sometimes, but I wouldn't say I have excessive worry or anxiety. I don't feel like my thoughts are out of control or anything. It's really just the exhaustion and that... that flat feeling I mentioned, rather than feeling anxious about things.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) - patient explicitly denies excessive worry and anxiety. Ruled out F48.8 (Other specified neurotic disorders) - clinical presentation is consistent with Major Depressive Disorder rather than a neurotic disorder. Patient meets criteria for depression: persistent depressed mood (gray film), anhedonia (loss of enjoyment), fatigue, and 3+ year duration.
